title: Anchor (ZIFFER-SPEC-001 §11.2, AU-3 / AU-3a / AU-4 / AU-7 / AU-8)
description:
The external commitment to one per-tenant audit chain head: what an anchoring party receives under AU-3, and what a verifier running outside the production trust domain compares its own recomputation against under AU-4. Carried on leg F6.4 of the leg register (ZIFFER-DEPLOY-001 Annex A); leg F6.3 carries the `chain_hash` this object commits to.

WHY THE OBJECT EXISTS AT ALL. AU-3 says it in one line: an unanchored in-database chain is tamper-DECORATED, not tamper-EVIDENT. The chain lives inside the production trust domain and a compromised audit writer can rewrite it; what such a writer cannot rewrite is an anchor already published. Everything below serves one comparison - recompute the head from the records under AU-1, then check it against what was anchored. AU-4 makes a head that fails to extend a previously anchored head a critical integrity alert, and AU-7 makes coverage by an anchor a precondition of releasing a floor-HIGH action rather than a report written afterwards.

NOTHING BELOW IS EVIDENCE ON ITS OWN (RES-8 / RES-9 / RES-10). Every field here is a value the publisher sends. The guarantee comes from two things outside this object: the store is append-only and sits outside the production trust domain (AU-4, ZIFFER-DEPLOY-001 DP-11), and the anchor is verifiable by any party holding the anchor public keys (AU-3a). A verifier that read a head from the chain it is auditing, or accepted an anchor because the audited party said it existed, has taken a derived security value from the party under verification - the class this architecture has hit five times, C2 -> X1 -> Y1 -> Z3 -> W1, each time inside machinery the previous fix introduced.

WHY THE FIELD SET IS CLOSED, AND WHY THAT IS A SECURITY PROPERTY. Every field is REQUIRED and `additionalProperties` is false. An anchor is a signed structure (CR-1), so an optional field gives one semantic anchor two canonical encodings, two signed preimages and two values - the Z4 defect that AT-8b closes for the Attestation Object one schema over. Here the consequence is worse than a duplicate id, because it lands on an honest party: a publisher that omits the field and a verifier that encodes it as absent-present compute different bytes, the signature fails, and AU-4 raises a critical integrity alert with no attacker anywhere. That is exactly what the AU-1 correction records happening to this subsystem already, from a formula rather than a field.

WHAT THIS SCHEMA DOES NOT MODEL, STATED SO THE FILE IS NOT READ WIDER THAN IT IS.
(1) The signature envelope. CR-2 makes a signature a map from primitive to signature value and CR-3 requires the supplied set to match the declared suite exactly. That map is keyed by the primitive names whose one home is `spec/schemas/bundle/signature.schema.json`, in the other schema root. A `$ref` crossing roots resolves now (ACP-78 M1, for a named scalar), so what still blocks the envelope is the OPEN MAP and not the reference: the generator's only rule for one is `x-acp-absent`, which states what the SIGNED POLICY says when a lookup misses, and a message carries no authority to answer that -- in the wire root such a rule is now carried as documentation and no accessor is generated from it. So the envelope is disclosed as absent rather than invented in a shape the specification never gave it. This follows the precedent of the sibling Attestation Object schema, which models the AT-1 body and not the surrounding `kind` / `attester` / `sig`.
(2) AU-3's mechanism and its evidence. AU-3 permits a public transparency log with inclusion proofs, a threshold signature from at least 3 independent parties, or RFC 3161 timestamping. Those three have incompatible evidence shapes - a Merkle inclusion proof, a set of party signatures, a CMS TimeStampToken - and no clause says which the anchor carries, how a verifier learns which was used, or which of the anchor public keys AU-3a means. An outside auditor cannot verify this object from its fields alone, and saying so is more useful than inventing a discriminator.
(3) Ordering and rate. AU-3's <= 10 min interval (L-19) and its at-every-bundle-activation rule are properties of a SEQUENCE of anchors; AU-4's extension check is a relation between two of them; AU-7's anchor-before-release is an ordering between an anchor and an execution. None is a property of one object and none is expressible here. They are per-implementation obligations (`spec/vectors/OBLIGATIONS.md`), and `reference/suites/audit_suite.py` is where the reference discharges them.
(4) AU-5 retention (>= 24 months or per regulation), AU-6 outage behaviour, and §11.3's eight reconciliation checks. All are about what a deployment does with anchors, never about what one is.

ENCODING, AND A GAP. §11.2 fixes `canonical()` for §11 as the single canonicaliser AT-8a requires - canonical CBOR, RFC 8949 §4.2 - and requires chain values to be carried, stored, anchored and fed forward as the 71-character `sha256:` string. That is the only canonicaliser §11 names, so it is the reading this schema is written against. But no clause states the anchor's own signed preimage: whether the signature covers this whole object, the `chain_hash` alone, or a mechanism-specific structure. AU-3a cannot hold until it is pinned, for the reason AU-1 already records - two implementations signing different bytes each refuse the other's anchor, and at the verifier a refusal is indistinguishable from tampering. JSON here is diagnostic form, never an accepted input.

tenant_id.description:
The tenant whose chain this anchor commits to. AU-1 makes chains per-tenant and AU-2 makes `(tenant_id, seq)` unique and gapless, so a head with no tenant names no chain: a verifier holding anchors from many tenants cannot tell which recomputation to compare against, and AU-4's extension check has no predecessor to look for.

It is a NAME for something already inside the chain, not a second source of it. AU-8 derives genesis from a tenant-creation record over `{tenant_id, created_at, bundle_epoch, schema_version}`, so the tenant is committed from `chain_hash_0` onward and a verifier that trusted this field over the chain would be trusting the publisher about which chain it published.

The specification pins no form for a tenant identifier - §9.2 renders one as `ten_04qf` in diagnostic JSON and no clause types it. The only stated bound is L-04 (max string field length 2,048 chars, no exceptions), so it is applied here rather than inventing a narrower one. That L-04's enforcement point is the Input/Output Schema registry and is being read as a general wire bound is an assumption; it is recorded rather than made quietly.

seq.description:
The sequence number of the record whose head is anchored. AU-2 makes `(tenant_id, seq)` unique and gapless per tenant, and gaplessness is what makes deletion detectable at all - a sequence with holes has no missing record, only a shorter one.

Zero is the genesis anchor. AU-8 requires it to be published IMMEDIATELY on tenant creation rather than on AU-3's <= 10 min schedule, because without an anchored genesis the destruction of an entire tenant chain is detectable only after the first scheduled anchor, and a chain destroyed inside that window leaves no evidence it ever existed.

An anchor at `seq` commits transitively to every record from 0 to `seq`, because AU-1 chains each head over the previous one. That is derived from the chain construction rather than promised by this field, and it is what §11.3(g) relies on when it asks for an anchor COVERING a floor-HIGH execution record.

chain_hash.description:
The anchored head: `chain_hash_seq` as AU-1 constructs it, `H({prev, record})` over the canonical encoding of a two-key map whose key names are part of the preimage. Carried as the 71-character string §11.2 pins, never as the 32 raw digest bytes - that type is pinned in the specification because an implementer who fed forward raw bytes built a different chain while following the text.

A NAME FOR A BINDING, NOT EVIDENCE OF ONE. The verifier's job under AU-4 is to recompute the head from the records and compare, so this value is one half of a comparison whose other half the verifier computes itself. It is trustworthy only to the degree that the store holding it is append-only and outside the production trust domain; the field carries no authority of its own.

THE AU-1 CORRECTION IS WHY THAT SENTENCE IS WORTH WRITING. Through v1.3.13 the clause read `SHA-256(chain_hash_{n-1} || canonical(record_n))`, a concatenation, while the reference hashed the canonical encoding of the two-key map. Different preimage, different chain from record 1 onward. The damage was not that an implementer failed to match: an honest third party implementing the clause literally recomputes a different head on an untampered chain, so AU-3a's independent verifiability did not hold, and AU-4 routed an honest verifier into this system's own critical-alert channel with no attacker present. The clause moved and the implementations did not, and the reasoning was published rather than taken silently.

anchored_at.description:
When the anchor was published. §11.3(g) requires every floor-HIGH execution record to be matched to an anchor DATED AT OR BEFORE release, and AU-7 makes that ordering a release precondition rather than a report, so the comparison needs a date and this is it.

WHO STAMPS IT IS THE WHOLE QUESTION, AND NO CLAUSE ANSWERS IT. If the anchoring party stamps it, the field is an external attestation of time and AU-7 means what it says. If the publisher stamps it, the party under verification dates its own alibi: a compromised audit writer backdates the anchor it has just published, and §11.3(g) - one of the mechanisms by which several disclosed residuals are said to be DETECTED rather than prevented - compares two numbers written by the same hand. Detection that can be erased is not detection, in AU-7's own words, and a timestamp the audited party chooses is erasure with an extra step. The Python reference is the second reading: `AnchorService.publish(tenant, seq, head, now)` in `reference/src/acp_audit.py` takes `now` from its caller, and the caller is `AuditChain.anchor_now`, inside the production trust domain. Recorded and filed; a schema cannot settle it.

THE TYPE IS NOT THE SPECIFICATION'S EITHER. No clause types an anchor timestamp. RFC 3339 is used because §9.2's `issued_at` and `expires_at` are RFC 3339 instants and §12.5 disciplines every receipt-issuing and receipt-verifying clock with NTS inside the L-20 skew allowance, so a second time format in the one subsystem whose value is retrospective would be a second encoding of one thing. The reference stores a POSIX float, so the two disagree today; that is a divergence to close in one place, not two.

alg.description:
The signature suite the anchor was signed under. CR-1 names the audit anchor explicitly among the structures that MUST carry an explicit `alg` identifying a suite registered in the signed bundle, and an unregistered or unknown suite MUST fail closed.

IT IS IN THE BODY BECAUSE OF WHAT HAPPENS WHEN IT IS NOT. PB-8 records the reasoning for the bundle SIGNATURE file and it transfers unchanged: the declared suite must be inside what the signature covers, or an attacker relabels a hybrid structure as classical, the verifier obligingly requires one primitive, and CR-3's conjunctive guarantee is decorative at the point it is loaded. An anchor is the structure a downgrade is worth most against - receipts live 120 s (L-14) and attestations 60 min (AT-1), while the audit chain's non-repudiation value is retrospective and measured in years, which is why §1 tells deployments to prioritise post-quantum signing on anchoring and bundle signing over receipt signing.

THE SUITE-NAME TYPE HAS ONE HOME AND IT IS NOT THIS FILE. The enumerated names are `SuiteId` at `spec/schemas/bundle/signature.schema.json#/$defs/suite_id`, in the other schema root, alongside the primitive names CR-2's signature map is keyed by. Declaring the enum a second time here would be two definitions of one object - the defect that generator exists to prevent, committed in a file that cites it. Where a type shared by both roots lives is now decided (ACP-78 M1): a named SCALAR is `$ref`d across roots and imported rather than redeclared, which is what the Decision Receipt's `alg` does. This field deliberately does NOT do that, and the reason is the conflict recorded below rather than a missing mechanism: AU-3 requires an EXTERNAL anchoring mechanism while CR-1/CR-4 require the deployment's registered floor, no public transparency log or timestamping authority signs under either registered suite, and typing this field as `SuiteId` would decide that conflict by writing a schema. So the constraint is stated and the type is pointed at rather than made in passing in a schema about anchors.

CR-4 IS SATISFIED BY CONTAINMENT, NEVER BY RANK, and the floor is read from the signed bundle rather than from this field. A verifier that ordered suites would place hybrid above `slhdsa128s` and serve a lattice signature to a deployment that chose hash-based precisely to rest on no lattice assumption. CR-6 SHOULD-recommends SLH-DSA for audit anchoring, and `slhdsa128s` is declared and not implemented in either implementation (ZIFFER-DEPLOY-001 DP-27), so a deployment following CR-6 to the letter cannot run today. That tension is the specification's and is named here rather than resolved by a schema.
